name: Treaty with the Chasta, etc., 1854
aka: Treaty with the Chasta, Scoton and Grave Creek Umpqua, November 18, 1854
nations: Quil-si-eton and Na-hel-ta bands of the Chasta (Shasta)
Cow-nan-ti-co, Sa-cher-i-ton and Na-al-ye bands of Scoton
Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde and Confederated Tribes of Siletz Indians (successors)
promises: Article 2: the bands to move to such part of the Table Rock reserve as the superintendent assigned, or to another reserve the President directed.
Article 3: $2,000 a year for fifteen years from September 1, 1855, added to and shared with the Rogue River annuities of the 1853 treaty, spent for the bands' benefit as the President prescribed.
Article 4: $6,500 for provisions in the first year on the reserve, buildings, and breaking and fencing fifty acres with seed.
Article 5: for all Indians on the reserve, a farmer for fifteen years, two blacksmith shops for five years, a hospital and medical care for ten years, and schools with teachers for fifteen years.
Article 6: the President could survey the reserve and assign farms of 20 to 80 acres as permanent homes.

breaches.what: The Court of Claims found that some funds Congress appropriated to meet this treaty's obligations were not spent for the bands as the treaty provided, and held the Chasta, Scotons and Grave Creek Band of Umpquas entitled to recover $10,224.34 plus $4,695.69 in administrative expense improperly charged to their funds, a total of $14,920.03, subject to offsets.

breaches.quote: funds actually appropriated to meet the obligations of the various treaties were not expended for the benefit of the Indians as provided

compensation: The annuities and services in Articles 3 to 5. In 1946 the Court of Claims held the Chasta, Scotons and Grave Creek Band of Umpquas entitled to $14,920.03 for unspent treaty funds and improperly charged administrative expense under this treaty. In 1950 it found that the gratuities the United States had spent for them up to July 1, 1943 equalled that award, so nothing was left to pay, and dismissed their petition (89 F. Supp. 798).
today: The Court of Claims found in 1946 that these bands, with the Rogue River Tribe, were placed on the Table Rock Reservation in 1854 and 1855 and most were moved to the Coast or Siletz Reservation in 1857; it held the United States had no treaty duty to give them a separate permanent reservation. The Western Oregon termination act of August 13, 1954 (68 Stat. 724) named the Shasta, Scoton, Grave and Galic Creek peoples among the tribes whose federal supervision was to end; the Table Rock reserve was set apart by the 1853 Rogue River treaty, not this one, so the Act is not counted as a breach here. The Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde and of Siletz Indians are successors.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribes list this treaty among the ratified and unratified treaties of the 1850s that ceded land from the Coast Range to the Cascades and resulted in the forced removal of tribal members from their homelands.

openQuestions: Whether the annuities and the Article 5 farmer, smiths, hospital and schools were provided after the Rogue River War of 1855-56 and the removal north was not researched.
The Grand Ronde treaties page names the Quilsieton and Nahelta bands of the Chasta and the Scoton bands for this treaty but not the Grave Creek band.
treaties.json lists the Cow Creek Band of Umpqua among present-day tribes; the Cow Creek had their own treaty of September 19, 1853. Not checked.

Audit 2026-11-08: both Rogue River Tribe opinions were read in full from the Caselaw Access Project. The 1946 opinion holds that appropriated funds under this treaty went unspent and awards $14,920.03; added as a court-ruling breach, so the file now meets the broken standard. The 1950 opinion found offsets for gratuities equal to the award and dismissed these bands' petition, so nothing was paid on the judgment.

The 1946 work-order holding (the Act of March 3, 1875 requiring labour for treaty annuities, called 'a plain violation' of the treaties) lists unpaid sums only under the 1853, November 29, 1854 and January 22, 1855 treaties, not this one.

plain.promised: The Chasta, Scoton and Grave Creek bands gave up their country on the Rogue River for a place on the Table Rock reserve, $2,000 a year for fifteen years, and a farmer, smiths, a hospital and schools.
plain.happened: In 1946 the Court of Claims found that money Congress set aside for this treaty was not spent for these bands as promised, and held them owed $14,920.03.
plain.today: In 1950 the court set off the government's gifts to the bands against that sum, found nothing left to pay, and dismissed their claim. Congress ended federal services to these peoples in 1954.
